September 2026: inventory is down year over year in both property types, which is the through-line. Condo days to contract fell hard (65 to 53), so the August 'you generally have more time' framing was narrowed to a comparison against houses rather than an absolute.
glanceLede: There is less on the market than a year ago in both property types. Beyond that, single-family homes and condos/townhomes are behaving like two different markets. Here is {{ dataMonth }} against {{ priorMonth }}, side by side.

Active single-family listings fell {{ s.sfh.m.inventory.pct | abspct }} to {{ s.sfh.m.inventory.current | int }} and condo/townhome listings fell {{ s.condo.m.inventory.pct | abspct }} to {{ s.condo.m.inventory.current | int }}, which pulled months of supply down on both sides.

Single-family supply at {{ s.sfh.m.monthsSupply.current | dec1 }} months is seller-leaning. Homes went under contract in a median {{ s.sfh.m.daysToContract.current }} days, down from {{ s.sfh.m.daysToContract.prior }}, even though closed sales slipped {{ s.sfh.m.closedSales.pct | abspct }}.

Condos and townhomes still offer more room at {{ s.condo.m.monthsSupply.current | dec1 }} months of supply, but less than they did: supply is down from {{ s.condo.m.monthsSupply.prior | dec1 }} months and contract time fell from {{ s.condo.m.daysToContract.prior }} days to {{ s.condo.m.daysToContract.current }}.

buyers.lede: The data points to a firmer single-family market and a condo/townhome market that still leaves room to negotiate, though less than a year ago. How you prepare depends on which one you are shopping.
sfh: Active single-family inventory is {{ s.sfh.m.inventory.current | int }}, down {{ s.sfh.m.inventory.pct | abspct }} from {{ s.sfh.m.inventory.prior | int }} a year ago. Set up alerts early and tour new listings promptly.
Be ready before you find the one.

Median days to contract is {{ s.sfh.m.daysToContract.current }}, down from {{ s.sfh.m.daysToContract.prior }}. Have a current pre-approval (or proof of funds), and decide in advance what matters most in inspection and appraisal terms.
Expect a gap between list price and sale price.
The typical sale closed at {{ s.sfh.m.olpReceived.current | dec1 }}% of its original list price. Use recent closed sales, not asking prices, to judge where an offer should start.
You may be competing with cash.
{{ cash.sfh }}% of single-family closings were cash (calculated). Financed buyers can compete on clean terms: solid pre-approval, reasonable timelines and a meaningful deposit.
condo: You generally have more room here than on a house.

At {{ s.condo.m.monthsSupply.current | dec1 }} months of supply against {{ s.sfh.m.monthsSupply.current | dec1 }} for single-family, and a {{ s.condo.m.daysToContract.current }}-day median to contract, there is usually room to ask for a price adjustment, credits or repairs.

Supply fell from {{ s.condo.m.monthsSupply.prior | dec1 }} to {{ s.condo.m.monthsSupply.current | dec1 }} months, inventory dropped {{ s.condo.m.inventory.pct | abspct }}, and contract time came down from {{ s.condo.m.daysToContract.prior }} days to {{ s.condo.m.daysToContract.current }}. The best-priced units in well-run buildings may not wait.
Use the time for due diligence.
Review the association budget, reserves, recent and planned assessments, and inspection records before you commit. The price is only part of the cost of a condo.
{{ cash.condo }}% of condo/townhome closings were cash (calculated). If you are financing, confirm early that your lender will lend in the specific building.

sellers.lede: Buyers are still paying below original list price in both segments, which makes the first price you choose one of the most important decisions you make.
sfh: Supply favors you. Pricing decides the outcome.

At {{ s.sfh.m.monthsSupply.current | dec1 }} months of supply, down from {{ s.sfh.m.monthsSupply.prior | dec1 }}, well-priced homes are going under contract in a median {{ s.sfh.m.daysToContract.current }} days. That speed tends to reward homes priced to recent closed sales.
Price from closed sales, not list prices.

The typical sale closed at {{ s.sfh.m.olpReceived.current | dec1 }}% of its original list price. Last year's prices and a neighbor's asking price are weak guides. A price that starts too high often has to come down later, after the listing has lost its first wave of attention.
{{ cash.sfh }}% of single-family closings were cash (calculated). Having disclosures, permits and recent service records ready makes it easier for any buyer, cash or financed, to move quickly.

Fewer closed sales ({{ s.sfh.m.closedSales.current | int }} vs. {{ s.sfh.m.closedSales.prior | int }}) means each buyer is choosing carefully. Repairs, cleaning and professional photography help your home compete.
condo: Plan for negotiation, but a shorter runway than last year.

At {{ s.condo.m.monthsSupply.current | dec1 }} months of supply most buyers will expect room to negotiate. Median days to contract fell from {{ s.condo.m.daysToContract.prior }} to {{ s.condo.m.daysToContract.current }}, so a well-priced unit should not sit as long as it would have in {{ priorMonth }}.
A higher median does not close the list-price gap.

Supply is down from {{ s.condo.m.monthsSupply.prior | dec1 }} months and the median price rose {{ s.condo.m.medianPrice.pct | abspct }} to {{ s.condo.m.medianPrice.current | usd }}, yet the typical sale still closed at {{ s.condo.m.olpReceived.current | dec1 }}% of original list price.
Have building paperwork ready on day one.
Budget, reserves, assessment history, insurance and inspection status are what serious condo buyers ask about first. Gathering them early prevents delays after you accept an offer.
Cash buyers are a large share of this market.
{{ cash.condo }}% of condo/townhome closings were cash (calculated). Clear terms and a straightforward closing timeline appeal to these buyers.
